lessons.title: Variables and Types
lessons.content:
# Variables and Types

```csharp
int xp = 100;
string name = "Ada";
bool isInstructor = true;
double score = 92.5;

Console.WriteLine($"{name} has {xp} XP");
```

## Common types

| Type | Example |
|------|---------|
| `int` | `42` |
| `double` | `3.14` |
| `string` | `"hello"` |
| `bool` | `true` / `false` |

## String interpolation

A `$"..."` string lets you embed expressions directly with `{ }`, this is called **string interpolation**.

## Type inference with `var`

```csharp
var count = 10; // the compiler infers count is an int
```

`var` doesn't make C# dynamically typed, the compiler still figures out and locks in a concrete type at compile time, it just saves you from writing it out.

questions.prompt: Which keyword lets the compiler infer a variable's type from its initial value?
Embedding expressions directly in a string with $"{name}" is called string ____.
Once a variable is declared as an int, you can later assign a string to it without casting or conversion.

lessons.title: Control Flow and Loops

questions.prompt: Which loop is the best fit for visiting every element of a collection without needing an index?
A for loop has three parts separated by semicolons: initializer, condition, and ____.
An if statement in C# requires its condition to evaluate to a boolean.

lessons.title: Methods and Classes

questions.prompt: What is the method that runs automatically when you create a new instance of a class called?
The ____ keyword allocates a new instance of a class and runs its constructor.
By convention, C# method names use PascalCase, like GainXp rather than gainXp.

lessons.title: Collections and LINQ

questions.prompt: Which LINQ method keeps only the elements that match a condition?
A resizable, generic collection of integers is declared as List<____>.
LINQ methods like Where and Select modify the original collection in place.

lessons.title: Final Project: Console Grade Book
lessons.content:
# Final Project: Console Grade Book

Time to combine classes, collections, and LINQ into a real console application.

## Requirements

1. Create a `Student` class with a name and a list of scores.
2. Store several students in a `List<Student>`.
3. Write a method that computes a student's average score.
4. Use LINQ (`Where`, `Select`, or similar) to filter and report which students are passing (e.g. average `>= 70`).
5. Loop over every student and print a report line with their name, average, and a letter grade (A/B/C/D/F) based on thresholds you define.

## Stretch goals

- Read student data from `Console.ReadLine()` instead of hardcoding it.
- Sort students by average score, highest first.
- Wrap score parsing in a `try/catch` to handle invalid input gracefully.

Submit your repository link below when you are done, an instructor will review it before you can mark this lesson complete. Good luck! 🚀
